mcqs.question: What pattern is actually doing the work underneath a DI container's construction of an object graph?
options: A Factory (or Abstract Factory) — the container decides which concrete classes to construct and supplies them, exactly like a hand-written factory, but automated across the whole graph
Observer, since the container notifies each class when its dependencies are ready
Decorator, since the container wraps each class in additional behavior
There is no underlying pattern — DI containers use an entirely novel mechanism
mcqs.explanation: A DI container automates exactly what a hand-written Factory does — deciding which concrete class to construct and wiring dependencies together — just scaled to an entire object graph instead of one class. There's no notification mechanism (ruling out Observer), no added wrapping behavior (ruling out Decorator), and the mechanism is a well-known pattern, not something novel.

mcqs.question: What's the core difference between Dependency Injection and the Service Locator anti-pattern?
options: DI can only be used with interfaces, while Service Locator can only be used with concrete classes
DI pushes dependencies into a class through its constructor; Service Locator has the class pull its dependency from a global registry inside a method body
Service Locator is simply a faster implementation of the same DI mechanism
DI and Service Locator differ only in which annotation library is used
mcqs.explanation: The core difference is push vs pull: DI supplies dependencies visibly through the constructor, while Service Locator has code reach out to a global registry from inside a method, hiding the dependency. Neither is restricted to interfaces vs concrete classes, performance isn't the distinguishing factor, and the difference isn't about annotation libraries.

mcqs.question: Why does Service Locator make unit testing harder than constructor injection?
options: Service Locator classes cannot be instantiated inside a unit test at all
Constructor injection requires a running application server to test, while Service Locator does not
Tests must configure a shared global registry with a mock before running the code, and reset it afterward, instead of simply passing a mock into a constructor
Unit testing frameworks like JUnit explicitly forbid testing classes that use Service Locator
mcqs.explanation: Service Locator forces tests into stateful setup and teardown around a shared global registry, whereas constructor injection just takes a mock as a plain parameter. Service Locator classes can be instantiated fine in tests, constructor injection doesn't require any application server, and JUnit has no such restriction.

mcqs.question: A container registers `PaymentService` with `singleton` scope. What pattern is this scope mechanism actually built on?
options: It's an entirely new pattern invented specifically for dependency injection containers
It's based on the Observer pattern, since the container notifies dependents when the singleton is ready
It's based on the Decorator pattern, wrapping the object with lifecycle management
It's a container-managed Singleton — the container constructs the bean once and hands out the same instance to every dependent
mcqs.explanation: Singleton scope is exactly Singleton's one-instance guarantee, just managed by the container instead of hand-rolled inside the class itself — which also sidesteps Singleton's usual testability problems. This isn't a new pattern, and neither Observer's notification model nor Decorator's wrapping behavior describes what scope management actually does.
